name: Chapter 1: Sets
description: Sets, roster and set-builder forms, subsets, intervals, Venn diagrams, union, intersection, complement and De Morgan’s laws.

cards.text: A set is a {{c1::well-defined}} collection of {{c2::objects}}.
cards.extra: Well-defined: for any object we can decide definitely whether it belongs or not.

cards.term: Is “the ten most talented writers of India” a set?
cards.definition: No: it is not well-defined: “most talented” depends on who is judging

cards.term: Is “the months of a year beginning with the letter J” a set?
cards.definition: Yes: {January, June, July}. Membership can be decided with certainty

cards.term: Objects, elements and members of a set: same or different?
cards.definition: Synonymous. Sets are named with capitals (A, B, X), elements with small letters (a, b, x)

cards.term: Read the symbols: \(a \in A\) and \(b \notin A\).
cards.definition: “a belongs to A” and “b does not belong to A”

cards.term: Symbols of standard number sets
cards.definition: N: natural numbers {1, 2, 3, …}; Z: integers {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …}; Q: rational numbers; T: irrational numbers (R − Q); R: real numbers; Z⁺, Q⁺, R⁺: positive integers, rationals, reals

cards.term: Does N include 0?
cards.definition: No: in NCERT, N = {1, 2, 3, …}. Z⁺ is the same set. Whole numbers W = {0, 1, 2, …}

cards.term: Two methods of writing a set?
cards.definition: Roster (tabular) form and set-builder form

cards.term: Roster form: rules?
cards.definition: List elements in braces { } separated by commas. Order does not matter; an element is not repeated

cards.term: Roster form of the set of letters in “SCHOOL”?
cards.definition: {S, C, H, O, L} (the repeated O is listed once; 5 elements)

cards.term: In {x : x is a vowel}, what do the braces and the colon mean?
cards.definition: Braces: “the set of all”. Colon: “such that”

cards.term: Set-builder form of the vowels V in English?
cards.definition: V = {x : x is a vowel in the English alphabet}

cards.term: Roster form of {x : x is a natural number and 3 < x < 10}?
cards.definition: {4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}

cards.term: Example: roster form of the solution set of x² + x − 2 = 0?
cards.definition: (x − 1)(x + 2) = 0 → {1, −2}

cards.term: Roster form of {x : x is a positive integer and x² < 40}?
Set-builder form of {1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …}?
cards.definition: {x : x = n², n ∈ N}, or “x is the square of a natural number”

\(\left\{x : x = \dfrac{n}{n+1},\ n \in \mathbb{N},\ 1 \le n \le 6\right\}\)
Numerator one less than denominator, n from 1 to 6

cards.term: Roster form of {x : x is an integer and −3 ≤ x < 7}?
cards.definition:
{−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
−3 is included, 7 is not

cards.term: Roster form of {x : x is a two-digit natural number with digit sum 8}?
cards.definition: {17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, 80} (8 elements)

cards.term: Roster form of {x : x is a prime divisor of 60}?
cards.definition: Prime factorisation 60 = 2² · 3 · 5 → {2, 3, 5}

cards.term: Roster form of the set of letters in TRIGONOMETRY?
cards.definition: {T, R, I, G, O, N, M, E, Y} (9 distinct letters)

cards.term: List {x : x is an integer, −½ < x < 9/2}.
cards.definition: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}

cards.term: List {x : x is an integer, x² ≤ 4}.
cards.definition:
{−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}
Trap: don’t forget the negatives.

cards.term: List {x : x is a month of a year not having 31 days}.
cards.definition: {February, April, June, September, November} (5)

cards.term: List {x : x is a consonant preceding k}.
cards.definition: {b, c, d, f, g, h, j}

cards.term: Match: {P, R, I, N, C, A, L} in set-builder form?
cards.definition: {x : x is a letter of the word PRINCIPAL}: 9 letters but P and I repeat, so 7 distinct
(a): x + 1 = 1 gives x = 0. (b) is {1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18}

cards.term: Which sets can never be written in roster form?
cards.definition: Sets whose elements follow no pattern, e.g. R (the real numbers) or the set of irrational numbers

cards.term: Define the empty set. Its symbol?
cards.definition: A set with no element. Called null or void set; written φ or { }

cards.term: Why is {x : 1 < x < 2, x ∈ N} empty?
cards.definition: There is no natural number between 1 and 2

cards.term: Why is {x : x² − 2 = 0, x rational} empty?
cards.definition: x = ±√2 is irrational: no rational solution

cards.term: Why is {x : x is an even prime greater than 2} empty?
cards.definition: 2 is the only even prime

cards.term: Why is {x : x² = 4, x odd} empty?
cards.definition: Solutions ±2 are even

cards.term: Is {x : x is a point common to two parallel lines} empty?
cards.definition: Yes: parallel lines never meet

cards.term: Trap: φ, {φ} and {0}: how many elements?
cards.definition: φ has 0; {φ} has 1 (the element is φ); {0} has 1 (the number 0)

cards.term: Intuition: an empty box, and a box that contains an empty box?
cards.definition: φ is the empty box (0 items). {φ} is a box holding an empty box (1 item). So n(φ) = 0 but n({φ}) = 1

cards.term: Is the empty set finite or infinite?
cards.definition: Finite: it has 0 elements. n(φ) = 0

cards.term: Define a finite set and an infinite set.
cards.definition: Finite: empty or has a definite number of elements. Infinite: otherwise

cards.term: What does n(S) denote?
cards.definition: The number of distinct elements of S

cards.term: Is the set of days of a week finite?
cards.definition: Finite: n(W) = 7

cards.term: Is the set of points on a line finite?
cards.definition: Infinite

First = {1, 2} → finite. Second: x = ½ ∉ N → φ → finite.
Empty sets are finite.

cards.term: Classify: {x ∈ N : x is prime} and {x ∈ N : x is odd}.
cards.definition: Both infinite (infinitely many primes, infinitely many odd numbers)

cards.term: Classify: the set of lines parallel to the x-axis; the set of circles through the origin.
cards.definition: Both infinite (y = c for any c; centres can be anywhere on suitable loci)

cards.term: Classify: the set of multiples of 5; the set of prime numbers less than 99.
cards.definition: Multiples of 5: infinite. Primes < 99: finite (25 of them, up to 97)

cards.term: Roster form of an infinite set: how?
cards.definition: Write a few elements showing the pattern followed by three dots, e.g. {1, 3, 5, 7, …}

cards.term: Define equal sets.
cards.definition: A = B if they have exactly the same elements (every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A)
Yes: order does not matter
Yes: repetition does not change a set

cards.term: Are the letter sets of ALLOY and LOYAL equal?
cards.definition: Yes: both are {A, L, O, Y}

cards.term: A = {x ∈ Z : x² ≤ 4}, B = {x ∈ R : x² − 3x + 2 = 0}: equal?
cards.definition: No: A = {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}, B = {1, 2}; 0 ∈ A but 0 ∉ B

cards.term: Prime numbers less than 6 and prime factors of 30: equal?
cards.definition: Yes: both are {2, 3, 5}

cards.term: Trap: is {0} = φ?
cards.definition: No: {0} has one element (0); φ has none

cards.term: From Ex 1.2: B = {1, 2, 3, 4} and D = {3, 1, 4, 2}; E = {−1, 1} and G = {1, −1}. Which are equal?
cards.definition: B = D and E = G

cards.term: Two sets: A = {x : x is a multiple of 10} and B = {10, 15, 20, 25, …}. Equal?
cards.definition: No: 15 ∈ B but 15 is not a multiple of 10

cards.term: Define a subset.
cards.definition: A ⊂ B if every element of A is also in B: a ∈ A ⇒ a ∈ B

cards.term: Read: A ⊂ B, A ⊄ B, ⇒, ⇔.
cards.definition: A is a subset of B; A is not a subset of B; implies; if and only if (iff)

cards.term: Every set is a subset of itself. True?
cards.definition: True: A ⊂ A

cards.term: Is the empty set a subset of every set?
cards.definition: Yes: φ ⊂ A for every A (agreed by definition)

cards.term: Intuition: why is φ a subset of every set?
cards.definition: To fail, φ would need an element that is not in A. φ has no elements, so nothing can fail: the condition holds vacuously

cards.term: A ⊂ B and B ⊂ A implies?
cards.definition: A = B. This is how equality is proved in set problems: show both inclusions

cards.term: Proper subset and superset?
cards.definition: A ⊂ B and A ≠ B: A is a proper subset of B, and B is a superset of A

cards.term: What is a singleton set?
cards.definition: A set with exactly one element, like {a}

cards.term: Notation note: ⊂ or ⊆?
cards.definition: NCERT writes ⊂ for “subset (may be equal)”. Many books and JEE papers use ⊆ for that and reserve ⊂ for proper subset; read the context

cards.term: Relations among N, Z, Q, R, T?
cards.definition: \(\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}\), T ⊂ R, N ⊄ T

cards.term: Define Q (rational numbers) in set-builder form.
cards.definition: \(\mathbb{Q} = \left\{x : x = \dfrac{p}{q},\ p, q \in \mathbb{Z},\ q \neq 0\right\}\)

cards.term: Define the set T of irrational numbers.
cards.definition: \(T = \{x : x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \notin \mathbb{Q}\} = \mathbb{R} - \mathbb{Q}\); e.g. √2, √5, π

cards.term: Trap: A ∈ B and B ⊂ C. Does A ⊂ C follow?
cards.definition: No. A = {1}, B = {{1}, 2}, C = {{1}, 2, 3}: A ∈ B ⊂ C, but 1 ∈ A and 1 ∉ C

cards.term: Ex 1.3 Q3: ∈ versus ⊂
cards.definition: {3, 4} ∈ A: True: {3, 4} is an element; {3, 4} ⊂ A: False: 3 ∉ A; {{3, 4}} ⊂ A: True: its only element {3,4} is in A; 1 ⊂ A: False: 1 is an element, not a set; {1, 2, 5} ⊂ A: True; {1, 2, 5} ∈ A: False: not an element; φ ∈ A: False: φ is not listed; φ ⊂ A: True; {φ} ⊂ A: False: φ ∉ A

{3, 4} ⊂ A?

1.6 · ∈ versus ⊂

A = {1, 2, {3, 4}, 5}. True or false?

{3, 4} ∈ ATrue: {3, 4} is an element
{3, 4} ⊂ AFalse: 3 ∉ A
{{3, 4}} ⊂ ATrue: its only element {3,4} is in A
1 ⊂ AFalse: 1 is an element, not a set
{1, 2, 5} ⊂ ATrue
{1, 2, 5} ∈ AFalse: not an element
φ ∈ AFalse: φ is not listed
φ ⊂ ATrue
{φ} ⊂ AFalse: φ ∉ A

Elements go with ∈. Sets go with ⊂. A set in braces inside A counts as one element.

cards.term: Trap: {a} ∈ {a, b, c} is true or false?
cards.definition: False: the elements are a, b, c. Correct: {a} ⊂ {a, b, c} or a ∈ {a, b, c}

cards.term: Is {a, b} ⊄ {b, c, a} true?
cards.definition: False: every element of {a, b} lies in {b, c, a}, so {a, b} ⊂ {b, c, a}

cards.term: List all subsets of {a, b}.
cards.definition: φ, {a}, {b}, {a, b}: 4 subsets

cards.term: List all subsets of {1, 2, 3}.
List all subsets of φ.
cards.definition: Only φ itself: 2⁰ = 1 subset

cards.term: List all subsets of {−1, 0, 1} by size.
Number of subsets of {a, b, c}: each element is in or out
cards.definition: A set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets: for each element choose in or out; {a,b,c} has 8

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Subsets · counting

How many subsets does {a, b, c} have, and why is the general answer 2ⁿ?

For each element you choose: in or out.

List all subsets of {a, b, c} before flipping.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Subsets · counting

How many subsets does {a, b, c} have, and why is the general answer 2ⁿ?

φ{a}{b}{c}{a, b}{a, c}{b, c}{a, b, c}

3 elements × (in / out) → 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 subsets.

General: n(P(A)) = 2ⁿ; proper subsets 2ⁿ − 1; non-empty proper 2ⁿ − 2.

cards.term: Number of subsets, proper subsets and non-empty proper subsets of a set with n elements?
Power set: definition and size?
cards.definition: P(A) = the set of all subsets of A; n(P(A)) = 2ⁿ

cards.term: Trap: what is P(φ), and how many elements has P(P(φ))?
cards.definition: P(φ) = {φ} (1 element). P({φ}) = {φ, {φ}} → 2 elements. A classic exam trap

cards.term: Types of intervals
cards.definition: (a, b): {x : a < x < b}  open; [a, b]: {x : a ≤ x ≤ b}  closed; [a, b): {x : a ≤ x < b}; (a, b]: {x : a < x ≤ b}

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

(a, b)?
[a, b]?
[a, b)?
(a, b]?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
1.6.2 · Intervals

Set-builder form of each interval.

(a, b){x : a < x < b} open
[a, b]{x : a ≤ x ≤ b} closed
[a, b){x : a ≤ x < b}
(a, b]{x : a < x ≤ b}

Square bracket includes the endpoint; round bracket excludes it.

cards.term: Length of the interval (a, b), [a, b], [a, b) or (a, b]?
cards.definition: b − a for every type

cards.term: Draw: how are open and closed endpoints marked on the number line?
cards.definition: Open circle ○ = excluded (round bracket); filled dot ● = included (square bracket)

cards.term: Interval (−1, 3] on the number line
cards.definition: (−1, 3] = {x ∈ R : −1 < x ≤ 3}. Round bracket → open circle (endpoint excluded). Square bracket → filled dot (endpoint included).

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval (−1, 3] on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

Which ends get a filled dot, which an open one?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval (−1, 3] on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

{x ∈ R : −1 < x ≤ 3}

Round bracket → open circle (endpoint excluded). Square bracket → filled dot (endpoint included).

cards.term: Closed interval [2, 6] on the number line
cards.definition: [2, 6] = {x ∈ R : 2 ≤ x ≤ 6}. Closed interval: both endpoints belong. Its length is b − a = 4.

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval [2, 6] on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

Which ends get a filled dot, which an open one?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval [2, 6] on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

{x ∈ R : 2 ≤ x ≤ 6}

Closed interval: both endpoints belong. Its length is b − a = 4.

cards.term: Interval [−2, ∞) on the number line
cards.definition: [−2, ∞) = {x ∈ R : x ≥ −2}. ∞ is not a number, so its side always takes a round bracket.

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval [−2, ∞) on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

Which ends get a filled dot, which an open one?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Intervals · number line

Draw the interval [−2, ∞) on the real line and write it in set-builder form.

{x ∈ R : x ≥ −2}

∞ is not a number, so its side always takes a round bracket.

cards.term: Why must ∞ always have a round bracket?
cards.definition: ∞ is not a number, so it can never be an endpoint that belongs to the set: (−∞, 3], [2, ∞)

cards.term: Interval for the non-negative reals? For the negative reals?
cards.definition: [0, ∞) and (−∞, 0)

cards.term: Write {x ∈ R : −5 < x ≤ 7} as an interval.
cards.definition: (−5, 7]

cards.term: Write [−3, 5) in set-builder form.
cards.definition: {x : −3 ≤ x < 5}

cards.term: Interval conversions

cards.definition: Yes: every real between −3 and 5 lies in [−7, 9]

cards.term: How many points does an interval contain?
cards.definition: Infinitely many, however short it is

cards.term: Intersection of intervals [1,5] ∩ (3,8)
cards.definition: [1,5] ∩ (3,8) = (3,5]; an endpoint stays only if it belongs to both intervals

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Intervals · intersection

A = [1, 5] and B = (3, 8). Find A ∩ B.

Think it through, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Intervals · intersection

A = [1, 5] and B = (3, 8). Find A ∩ B.

A ∩ B = (3, 5]: the stretch where both bands are present.

At 3: in A but not in B → excluded. At 5: in both → included.

Trap: the endpoint is in the intersection only if it is in both sets.

cards.term: Union of intervals [1,5] ∪ (3,8)
cards.definition: [1,5] ∪ (3,8) = [1,8); two intervals merge only if they overlap or touch with an included point

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Intervals · union

Same A = [1, 5] and B = (3, 8). Find A ∪ B.

Think it through, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Intervals · union

Same A = [1, 5] and B = (3, 8). Find A ∪ B.

A ∪ B = [1, 8): the bands overlap, so they join into one interval.

Left end 1 comes from A (closed), right end 8 from B (open).

Trap: (1, 3) ∪ (3, 5) is not (1, 5): the point 3 is missing.

cards.definition: No: 3 is in neither open interval, so it is missing. The union is (1, 5) − {3}

\((0, 2)\)
0 is not in (0, 6]; 2 is not in [−3, 2)
R: the point 4 is covered by the second interval
{2}: a single point

cards.term: What is a universal set?
cards.definition: The basic set in a given context of which all sets under discussion are subsets. Denoted U

cards.term: Suggest a universal set for right triangles and for isosceles triangles.
cards.definition: The set of all triangles in a plane (both are subsets of it)

cards.term: Is the universal set unique?
cards.definition: No: for integers, U can be Q or R. Any set that contains all the sets in the problem will do
Only (iii) {0, 1, …, 10}. It must contain 0 (from C) and 8 (from C), and 1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6: (i) lacks 8, (iv) lacks 0

cards.term: How does a Venn diagram show sets?
cards.definition: Rectangle = universal set; circles inside it = subsets. Named after John Venn (1834–1883)

cards.term: In a Venn diagram, how is B ⊂ A drawn?
cards.definition: Circle B lies completely inside circle A

cards.term: How are disjoint sets drawn?
cards.definition: Two circles that do not overlap

cards.term: Venn shading: A ∪ B
cards.definition: A ∪ B is both circles together, the overlap included

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A ∪ B on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A ∪ B on a Venn diagram.

A ∪ B = everything in A or B (or both): the two whole circles.

cards.term: Venn shading: A ∩ B
cards.definition: A ∩ B is only the overlapping lens

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A ∩ B on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A ∩ B on a Venn diagram.

A ∩ B = in A and B: only the lens where the circles overlap.

cards.term: Venn shading: A − B
cards.definition: A − B is the part of A outside B (equals A ∩ B′)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A − B on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A − B on a Venn diagram.

A − B = in A but not in B: A’s crescent with the overlap removed.

Also written A ∩ B′.

cards.term: Venn shading: A′
cards.definition: A′ is everything in U outside A

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A′ (complement of A) on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A′ (complement of A) on a Venn diagram.

A′ = U − A: everything in the rectangle outside circle A, including all of B that is not in A.

cards.term: Venn shading: (A ∪ B)′
cards.definition: (A ∪ B)′ is the region outside both circles

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade (A ∪ B)′ on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade (A ∪ B)′ on a Venn diagram.

(A ∪ B)′ = the region outside both circles.

cards.term: Venn shading: (A ∩ B)′
cards.definition: (A ∩ B)′ is everything except the overlap lens

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade (A ∩ B)′ on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade (A ∩ B)′ on a Venn diagram.

(A ∩ B)′ = everything except the overlap lens: it does include the crescents of A and B.

cards.term: Venn shading: symmetric difference
cards.definition: A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A): in exactly one of A, B; n = n(A)+n(B)−2n(A∩B)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A Δ B (symmetric difference) on a Venn diagram.

Picture the shaded region, then flip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Venn diagrams · shade it

Shade A Δ B (symmetric difference) on a Venn diagram.

A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A): in exactly one of the sets, i.e. both circles minus the lens.

n(A Δ B) = n(A) + n(B) − 2·n(A ∩ B)

cards.term: Define A ∪ B.
cards.definition: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}; common elements are written once
{2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}

cards.term: Interpret X ∪ Y, X = hockey team, Y = football team of Class XI.
cards.definition: Students in the hockey team or the football team or both

cards.term: Mnemonic for ∪ and ∩?
cards.definition: ∪ looks like a “U” for Union and means or. ∩ means and (∧ without the bar)

cards.term: If B ⊂ A, then A ∪ B = ?
cards.definition: A

cards.term: Laws of union
cards.definition: A ∪ B = B ∪ A: Commutative; (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C): Associative; A ∪ φ = A: Identity (φ is the identity of ∪); A ∪ A = A: Idempotent; A ∪ U = U: Law of U

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
1.9.1 · Properties of union

Name the law.

A ∪ B = B ∪ A?
(A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C)?
A ∪ φ = A?
A ∪ A = A?
A ∪ U = U?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
1.9.1 · Properties of union

Name the law.

A ∪ B = B ∪ ACommutative
(A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C)Associative
A ∪ φ = AIdentity (φ is the identity of ∪)
A ∪ A = AIdempotent
A ∪ U = ULaw of U

cards.term: Define A ∩ B.
cards.definition: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}: elements common to both
{6, 8}

cards.term: X = {Ram, Geeta, Akbar}, Y = {Geeta, David, Ashok}. X ∩ Y?
cards.definition: {Geeta}

cards.term: If B ⊂ A, then A ∩ B = ?
cards.definition: B

cards.term: When are A and B disjoint?
cards.definition: When A ∩ B = φ (no common element)

cards.term: Laws of intersection
cards.definition: A ∩ B = B ∩ A: Commutative; (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C): Associative; φ ∩ A = φ,  U ∩ A = A: Laws of φ and U; A ∩ A = A: Idempotent; A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C): Distributive: ∩ over ∪

cards.term: State De Morgan’s laws.

(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′
The complement of a union is the intersection of complements, and vice versa

cards.term: Mnemonic for De Morgan’s laws?
cards.definition: Break the bar, change the sign: break the bar over the bracket and swap ∪ ↔ ∩ (and complement each piece)

cards.term: De Morgan: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (Venn reasoning)
cards.definition: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′: not in the union means outside A and outside B; the outside-A and outside-B regions overlap only outside both circles

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
De Morgan’s law 1 · intuition

Why is (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ ?

Shade each side and compare.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
De Morgan’s law 1 · intuition

Why is (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ ?

Not in (A or B) = not in A and not in B.

Red = outside A, blue = outside B; purple (both) = outside both circles.

cards.term: De Morgan: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ (Venn reasoning)
cards.definition: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′: failing to be in both means being outside A or outside B, which covers everything except the lens

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
De Morgan’s law 2 · intuition

Why is (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ ?

Shade each side and compare.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
De Morgan’s law 2 · intuition

Why is (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ ?

Not in (A and B) = outside A or outside B.

Red + blue cover everything except the lens.

Trick: break the bar, flip the sign.

cards.term: Method: how do you prove two sets are equal?
cards.definition: Element chase: take x ∈ A and show x ∈ B (so A ⊂ B); then take x ∈ B and show x ∈ A. Conclude A = B

cards.term: Example 25: A ∪ B = A ∩ B ⇒ A = B. The trick?
cards.definition: Any a ∈ A lies in A ∪ B = A ∩ B, so a ∈ B; likewise any b ∈ B lies in A. Hence A ⊂ B and B ⊂ A

cards.term: Misc Q4: four equivalent conditions for A ⊂ B?
cards.definition: A − B = φ, A ∪ B = B, A ∩ B = A, and B′ ⊂ A′

cards.term: Misc Q3: A ∪ B = A ∪ C and A ∩ B = A ∩ C ⇒ B = C. Idea?
cards.definition: Write B = B ∩ (A ∪ B) = B ∩ (A ∪ C) = (B ∩ A) ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∩ C) ∪ (B ∩ C) = C ∩ (A ∪ B) = C ∩ (A ∪ C) = C

cards.term: Misc Q6: A = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A − B). Why?
cards.definition: Split A into the part inside B and the part outside B. Also A ∪ (B − A) = A ∪ B

cards.term: Absorption laws?

cards.term: Trap (Misc Q8): does A ∩ B = A ∩ C imply B = C?

cards.term: Trap: if x ∈ A and A ∈ B, is x ∈ B?
cards.definition: No. x = 1, A = {1}, B = {{1}}: 1 ∈ A, A ∈ B, but 1 ∉ B. Membership is not transitive; ⊂ is

Track how many times the middle region is counted.

Survey problem

In a class of 100, 60 like tea, 45 like coffee, 25 like both. How many like neither?

n(U) = 100, n(T) = 60, n(C) = 45, n(T ∩ C) = 25
  1. n(T ∪ C) = 60 + 45 − 25 = 80
  2. ?
  3. Only tea = 60 − 25 = 35; only coffee = 45 − 25 = 20
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Survey problem

In a class of 100, 60 like tea, 45 like coffee, 25 like both. How many like neither?

n(U) = 100, n(T) = 60, n(C) = 45, n(T ∩ C) = 25
  1. n(T ∪ C) = 60 + 45 − 25 = 80
  2. Neither = outside the union: n(U) − n(T ∪ C) = 100 − 80 = 20
  3. Only tea = 60 − 25 = 35; only coffee = 45 − 25 = 20
